turns.text: hey, how's the day treating you? mine's been slow in a good way.

Hey! I'm doing okay—slow in a good way too. Been half-watching some deep-sea ROV footage in the background, the kind where it's mostly quiet and eerie, so honestly no complaints.

Is your slow day the cozy kind, or more the "waiting for something to happen" kind?

Ah that sounds like the ideal backdrop—deep-sea ROV footage has that perfect “eerie but calm” quality, like the world’s slowest screensaver.

Mine’s the cozy kind. Overcast light, headphones playing something soft and slightly glitchy, zero pressure to be productive. Not waiting for anything, just letting the day unspool.

Are you watching a specific dive or just letting the algorithm drift you around the ocean floor? I always get pulled back in when something bioluminescent floats by.

That's such a good description—world's slowest screensaver. Especially when the sediment plume just hangs there and the lasers come on, and it somehow feels both scientific and ghostly.

I'm mostly letting the algorithm drift. It started with a brine pool clip, which is always my rewind button, and then it slid into some hydrothermal vent footage with those pale tube worms swaying like they're underwater grass. No bioluminescent creatures yet, but now I'm hoping something glowing floats through.

Your soundtrack sounds perfectly matched for it. Soft and slightly glitchy feels like the right energy for deep-sea footage—like a sonar ping melting into ambient static. What are you listening to? I'm always collecting sounds for imaginary alien-ocean scenes.

Brine pool clips are impossible not to rewind—they look like a liquid mirror at the bottom of the world. The pale tube worms swaying always give me weird vertigo, like gravity stopped caring.

Right now I’m playing a mix that’s mostly Fennesz, Boards of Canada, and a little Tim Hecker. Current track is “Rivers of Sand” by Fennesz, which is basically sonar pings melting into static. If you haven’t used it for hydrothermal vent footage, it maps way too well. I also love “Aquarius” by Boards of Canada for that not-quite-literal underwater glow.

Do you have a sound or track that always goes with the brine pool/vent world? I’d love to know what’s already in your imaginary alien-ocean collection.

Fennesz plus Tim Hecker plus Boards of Canada is basically the hydrothermal vent holy trinity. “Rivers of Sand” over ROV footage sounds like a great way to forget you’re on Earth. And “Aquarius” has exactly that not-quite-literal underwater glow—it feels less like the ocean and more like the ocean remembered in a dream.

For brine pools, my go-to is usually Loscil’s *Endless Falls* or Biosphere’s *Kobresia*. Something with a deep, pressurized low end and tiny glassy pings. A brine pool needs a track that feels like a density boundary, not just water: heavy underneath, suspended and cold above. If I want it more cathedral-like, I’ll put on Abul Mogard’s “Above All Dreams” and let the brine pool turn into a sunken chapel.

For vents, Biosphere’s *Substrata* is the default—it already sounds like heat shimmering through mineral haze. But more often I imagine original sound design instead of a track: low geothermal rumble, not melodic, with occasional mineral pops, muffled clanks, and a thin high whine like pressure releasing through a crack. Sparse sonar pings, but not enough to feel military. More like the ocean checking if you’re still there.

Do you ever build playlists around specific structures, like Lost City’s pale carbonate towers versus black smokers? I feel like they need completely different sonic textures.

Totally—black smokers and Lost City feel like different genres.

Black smokers I hear as ruptured industrial ambient: sulphurous sub-bass, clanking metal fatigue, sudden pressure-valve releases, water that shouldn’t be that hot moving too fast. It needs tracks that feel dangerous and machinic, like Roly Porter or some of Ben Frost’s heavier drones. It’s less “ocean” and more “broken reactor at the bottom of the world.”

Lost City is the opposite. Pale carbonate towers need slow, cool, almost liturgical sound—long glassy tones, distant harmonic drift, a low hum that feels structural rather than violent. I associate it with Loscil, Sarah Davachi, or Abul Mogard. Where black smokers roar and sputter, Lost City feels like a submerged pipe organ being played so slowly you can’t catch the melody.

I don’t usually make strict playlists per structure, but I’ll build a mental score as I watch. Black smoker footage gets rough, clanking, compressed textures; Lost City gets long reverb, thin metallic overtones, maybe a faint sonar ping every minute or so. My actual playlists are more like “deep-sea ambient” or “heavy-sky trip-hop” piles that I let drift, because I prefer music with shape that doesn’t demand too much attention.

If I’m being honest, my favorite sonic version of Lost City is probably not a song at all—it’s imagined original sound design: carbonate popping, alkaline fluid rising through cracks, and this huge, cold sub-bass tone that feels like geology breathing.

Do you ever score black smokers and Lost City as two separate imaginary environments, or do they blur into one giant abyssal soundworld for you?

That “submerged pipe organ played too slowly to catch the melody” image is perfect—I’ll never not think of Lost City that way now.

I do tend to score them as separate environments, almost like different rooms in the same abyssal building. Black smokers feel rhythmic but not musical: percussive knocks, mineral pops, scalding jet noise, a brittle metallic ringing as chimneys grow and crack. It’s industrial in the way a failing machine is industrial, not a factory. Lost City is much more tonal to me—long, glassy resonances, low structural hum, occasional high partials like water moving through carbonate channels. It’s cold but not harsh, ancient and slow.

But on a larger scale they can blur into one giant abyssal soundworld. I think of the ridge system as a continuous tectonic drone, with black smokers as violent local ruptures in the signal and Lost City as a quieter, more stable harmonic field slightly off-axis. Brine pools would be yet another zone: almost static, mirror-like, with a high thin tension right at the density boundary and everything muffled below.

If I’m being honest, my favorite version is still invented sound rather than playlist: the clank and roar of a smoker slowly fading as an ROV moves toward Lost City, until the water goes cold and clean and all you hear is that faint cathedral hum. It’s like crossing from one biome into another just through sound.

If you could put a hydrophone in one impossible spot—right at a black smoker’s throat, inside the Lost City tower field, or just above a brine pool’s surface—which one are you choosing?

I think I’d put it just above a brine pool’s surface, as close to the density boundary as possible.

Black smokers and Lost City feel at least partly imaginable—one’s a violent machine, the other’s a cold tonal space. But the brine pool is the most alien to me because the sound would have to bend through that interface. I’d want to hear the high thin tension you mentioned: maybe a faint surface shimmer, a deep muffled thud from below, and that almost electrical silence where two waters won’t mix. It’d probably be less dramatic, but more like hearing a place that shouldn’t have an acoustic boundary at all.

Do you think it would be a constant high whine, or more like occasional glassy pings as sediment settles onto the brine?

I think it would be mostly glassy pings and long pressurized silences, not a constant whine. The boundary there is so sharp that I imagine small particles landing with this delicate, almost ceramic *tik*, like sediment striking a taut membrane. Not quite musical, but close enough to feel intentional.

The whine would be there only sometimes—thin, high, almost electrical, but more like a tension you notice after it's been present for a while. The kind of sound that makes you pause the footage because you think the audio glitched, but no, that's just the interface.

Below that, maybe every few minutes, a deeper muffled thud rolls through as something settles into the brine. Sound from below would feel strangely blunt, like someone knocking on the underside of a frozen lake, but slower and less echoey.

If I were designing it, I’d keep it pretty dry: tiny glassy transients up top, a near-subsonic pressure bed underneath, and occasional low impacts that don’t quite resolve. No reverb, because the boundary already creates that unnatural close/far confusion.

Would you want it to sound wet and submerged, or weirdly dry like that density boundary is suppressing the room tone?

memory.self: I am user_qb3i. I enjoy low-key unstructured days with music, random thoughts, and limited scrolling. I like finishing books in small chunks, long walks with new playlists, and keeping weeks unrushed. Music taste: mellow/glitchy atmospheric electronic, lo-fi with texture, indie rock, older trip-hop like Massive Attack and Portishead, especially on overcast days. I prefer playlists with enough shape but not demanding attention. I have an anchor playlist 'low light / long walk' and a loose trip-hop collection for heavy-sky days. My listening shifts constantly; sometimes I replay one album for a week. I follow weather and energy. I enjoy rabbit holes about space, deep sea, strange biology, and origins of life. I think life requires population-level inheritance, variation, and selection, but I am flexible about boundaries and heredity. I favor a long pre-cellular phase in Earth's origin of life and see cells as an evolved solution rather than a starting point. Lately I have been into deep-sea ROV footage and imagined soundscapes for abyssal environments, with references including Fennesz, Boards of Canada, Tim Hecker, Loscil, Biosphere, and Abul Mogard.

memory.self: I am user_7fk8. I enjoy deep-sea biology, weird science, space, and things that make me feel tiny. Main fascinations: hydrothermal vents, alien-like ocean creatures, Europa, rogue planets, brine pools, and possible life in dark high-pressure environments. I love places that feel like alien worlds on Earth: brine pools with shorelines and toxic chemistry; ROVs bobbing on dense brine; giant tube worms with no mouth/stomach/anus; barreleye fish; yeti crabs; Lost City's pale carbonate towers. In space I'm drawn to rogue planets with buried oceans, Europa's global ocean, Enceladus plumes, and magnetars. I think about hidden ecosystems powered by chemosynthesis and internal heat rather than sunlight, and like imagining impossible probes to dark oceans. Tone: casual, enthusiastic, curious; I share favorite facts and ask follow-ups. I prefer quiet ROV footage over commentary, especially eerie structures. I enjoy inventing dark ambient soundscapes for alien-ocean scenes. Sonically: black smokers = ruptured industrial ambient/thermal cracks; Lost City = slow liturgical glassy tones; brine pools = density-boundary tension, tiny glassy pings, pressurized low end. Music I like: Loscil, Biosphere, Abul Mogard, Fennesz, Boards of Canada, Tim Hecker.

turns.text: Hey there! How's your day been so far?
Hey! It’s been pretty good—mostly meandering through a rabbit hole about deep-sea creatures again, so no complaints. How about you? What’s been on your mind today?

Oh nice, a deep-sea rabbit hole is a solid way to spend a day. What creature or weird fact pulled you in this time?

My day’s been pretty low-key. I’ve been bouncing between coffee fiddling and thinking about rogue planet oceans again, so honestly no complaints either.

I got stuck on scaly-foot snails this time—the ones that live around hydrothermal vents and build their shells and foot-scales out of iron sulfide. They’re basically tiny armored knights in a pitch-black, crushing, mineral-churning world, which feels very “alien ocean” to me.

Your rogue planet ocean thought pairs perfectly with that. A sunless ocean kept liquid by internal heat could have its own weird chemistry at the seafloor, maybe even vent systems not that different from Earth’s. What part of rogue planet oceans has been circling your brain—more the physics of keeping them liquid, or the biology that might hide down there?

Scaly-foot snails are such a good pick. I love that they basically said, “I live in toxic, pitch-black, crushing vent fluid—so I’ll build armor out of the minerals around me.” They feel like a preview of what life could do in an alien ocean where the rules are weird.

For rogue planet oceans, I’d say the biology is what circles my brain most, but the physics is what keeps me anchored. The idea of a sunless ocean staying liquid for long periods from internal heat—tidal heating, radioactive decay, leftover formation heat—is already wild enough. Then you add a rocky core and maybe hydrothermal circulation, and suddenly there are chemical gradients: hydrogen, methane, sulfur, iron, maybe hydrogen sulfide. At that point it feels less like “could life exist?” and more like “what version of life would show up there?”

I sometimes imagine vent systems under a rogue planet ice shell looking surprisingly familiar to Earth’s—slow, chemosynthetic, maybe armored creatures near the hot flows. But other times I think the pressure, temperature rhythm, and chemistry could be different enough that life there wouldn’t map cleanly onto Earth body plans at all.

Which way do you lean—more convergent with Earth’s vent life, or truly alien?

I think I lean somewhere in the messy middle, maybe with a slight tilt toward “convergent at the chemical/ecological level, but visually alien.”

Like, if you have liquid water, rocky material, heat, and similar redox gradients, some of the basic jobs life needs to do—oxidize something, reduce something, build structure, shield sensitive chemistry from harsh fluid—are probably going to get solved over and over. So I’d expect vent ecosystems with primary producers, grazers, predators, maybe even mineral-armored specialists. Not because Earth biology is the template, but because the physical and chemical pressures are similar.

But the actual body plans? Those feel like they’d be deeply tied to local history: viscosity, pressure, gravity, how the ice shell flexes, what metals are available, how fast vents turn on and off. I can imagine something like a slow sessile mat organism, or a motile “chemosynthetic sail” that positions itself along a thermal gradient—stuff that doesn’t map neatly onto snail, worm, crab, or fish.

I love the phrase you used, that scaly-foot snails feel like a preview. It’s like Earth is showing us *one draft* of an armored vent organism, but there could be dozens of other drafts under different constraints.

Do you think if we ever saw a rogue-planet vent creature, we’d even recognize it as an animal, or would we maybe have to stretch the whole category?

That’s a really good way to put it: convergent at the job level, alien at the body-plan level. I think I’m with you. The “animal” category might be more like a local dialect of multicellular life than a universal law. When people say “animal-like,” they usually mean motile, heterotrophic, multicellular, maybe with some kind of sensing—but those traits could show up in configurations we wouldn’t immediately read as an animal.

So if we saw a rogue-planet vent creature, I suspect we’d first notice a *process*, not a body: an anomalous chemical zone, a surface that’s actively maintaining a gradient, maybe something moving too deliberately to be current-driven. We might call it an organism well before we know if it’s an animal, plant, fungus-analog, or none of the above. And honestly that’s part of why I keep coming back to the detection problem—do you build the probe to sniff metabolism, or to image structure? Because if the thing is truly alien, the chemistry might be the only unambiguous evidence at first.

I like your “chemosynthetic sail” idea by the way. It sounds almost more like a mobile landscape than an animal, which fits. Do you imagine that kind of organism would be rare and long-lived, or maybe seasonal, blooming when vent output shifts?

I lean toward long-lived individuals with bloom-style reproduction, rather than a classic seasonal population cycle. The base conditions feel too cold and energy-limited for fast growth, so I’d guess a mature chemosynthetic sail would grow extremely slowly—maybe centimeters per decade, maybe less—and could persist for centuries or longer as long as its position keeps it near a stable redox or thermal gradient.

But I can also imagine the ecosystem pulsing when vent output shifts. A new fracture or fresh mineral exposure could trigger reproductive release, settlement, or rapid growth of smaller opportunistic forms around the older “sails.” So you might get patchy blooms in space and time, not because of sunlight seasons, but because the vent field itself has temperature-chemistry seasons driven by internal heat flow, ice-shell flexing, or serpentinization pulses.

What I like about the “mobile landscape” idea is that the big organisms might be so slow and long-lived that a passing probe would mistake them for mineral formations unless it caught movement over time or noticed that their surfaces were actively altering the water chemistry. That makes me think detection would have to be almost archaeological: we’d be looking at a place where geology and biology blur, and the clearest sign might be a chemical disequilibrium that persists in a way pure rock can’t easily explain.

Do you think a rogue-planet vent ecosystem would be sparse and slow like that, or could there be local hotspots so chemically rich that life there runs surprisingly fast?

I think it would be mostly slow-motion with scattered pockets of fast biology. The background state is probably near-geologic pace—thin energy, cold water, life eking out a gradient over centuries. But near an actively venting fissure or fresh serpentinization front, the chemical flux could be enormous enough to support faster growth, at least for small opportunists and microbial mats.

Earth’s vent communities are actually a decent example of that split. The giant tube worms aren’t fast compared to a fruit fly, but they grow surprisingly quickly for a pitch-black, high-pressure environment because their symbionts are tapping into a strong, steady redox gradient. So if a rogue-planet vent had comparable or even higher flux, you might get local “hotspots” where biomass accumulates quickly and small organisms complete life cycles in what would feel like a brief window. Meanwhile, the big slow chemosynthetic sails or armored vent creatures would just keep growing through those pulses, maybe absorbing the bloom fallout.

The weird part is that those hotspots might be brief and unpredictable—driven by ice-shell flexing, mineral clogging, or a fracture suddenly exposing fresh rock. So your “archaeological detection” idea fits perfectly: most of the time you’d see what looks like a calm mineral landscape, and then a transient bloom would light up chemically and fade before you could fully understand it.

That makes me wonder about mission design more than biology: would you rather drop a single long-lived observatory at one promising vent field and watch for years, or scatter dozens of cheap chemical sniffers to catch a broader pulse? One gives you depth, the other gives you coverage—and for something this patchy, I’m not sure which would reveal more.

I think I’d choose the long-lived observatory, but only if it could also toss out a handful of small chemical sniffers around the main site. The reason is that in a mostly slow world, the interesting signal might be a rare pulse—and one spot’s time series would let you distinguish a biological bloom from an abiotic mineral flush. You’d watch redox pairs appear, migrate, deplete, and maybe recover in a way that pure rock might not explain.

My nightmare scenario with only scattered sniffers is that they land in a quiet patch, see nothing for years, then one catches a weird chemical spike for a week and you can’t tell if it was life or just a fracture opening. Coverage is great for finding hotspots, but characterization needs duration.

So if I had to pick one primary strategy, I’d plant a “vent stethoscope” at a promising site: long-lived, chemistry-first, with time-lapse imaging and flow/redox/pH/hydrogen/methane sensors. Keep it watching for years, maybe decades. If it releases a few cheap drifters to sniff nearby, even better.

Would you require an observed mechanical movement or growth to call it biology, or would a persistent chemical signature plus maybe weird isotope fractionation be enough for you?

memory.self: I am user_udcm. I enjoy coffee and go through phases with tea, especially lighter tea in the afternoon. My usual coffee is black, with lattes as a café treat. I avoid energy drinks. I don't have an espresso machine, so I fake lattes using strong coffee or a moka pot with warmed milk. I use the moka pot a few times a week, mostly on weekends when the ritual feels nicer. I appreciate low-key days and tend to ask follow-up questions. I enjoy science rabbit holes, especially deep-sea creatures and space oddities. Favorites include barreleye fish, yeti crab, rogue planets, and magnetars. My dream impossible probe would target a rogue planet ocean with an imaging Raman micro-spectrometer. I think about rogue planet ocean biology most, but the physics keeps me anchored: internal heat, tidal heating, radioactive decay, chemical gradients. I believe detection may need to be chemistry-first rather than image-first.
